title: Min Cost Climbing Stairs
statement: You are given an array cost where cost[i] is the price you pay to step off step i. From a step you may climb one or two steps. You may start on step 0 or on step 1, and you must reach the floor past the last step. Return the minimum total price paid.
realWorld: Cheapest route through a chain of weighted positions where you may skip at most one: a build pipeline where each stage costs minutes and some stages can be jumped by a combined check, or a toll road where every exit charges and you may skip one booth at a time. It is the smallest interesting shortest-path problem — a path on a line.

examples.explanation: Start on step 1, pay 15, and climb two steps — that lands past the last step, so nothing more is paid. Starting at step 0 would cost 10 + 20 = 30 or 10 + 15 + 20 = 45.
Start on step 0, pay 1, climb two steps and you are past the end. You never pay for the last step because you never step off it.
Start on step 0 and pay at steps 0, 2, 4, 6, 7 and 9 — six payments of 1 each, dodging both 100s by choosing when to take a double step.

constraints: You may begin at index 0 or index 1
The goal is the position just past the last index

bruteForce.idea: Recursion straight from the wording: the cheapest finish from step i is cost[i] plus the cheaper of finishing from i + 1 and from i + 2. Start the recursion at both legal starting points and take the smaller.
code: private static int from(int[] cost, int i) {
return cost[i] + Math.min(from(cost, i + 1), from(cost, i + 2));
bruteForce.whySlow: The call tree branches in two at every step, and nothing remembers an answer. from(i) is re-evaluated once for every distinct route that arrives at step i, and the number of such routes is a Fibonacci number: for a 30-step staircase from(2) is computed over 500,000 times, and each of those evaluations produces the identical number. The staircase below step i does not care how you got to i, so all but one of those evaluations is pure repetition.

patternIdentification: You are asked for an optimum over a sequence of local decisions, and the options at a position depend only on which positions can reach it — not on the route taken to get there. That is the signature of one-dimensional DP. Write the state as a sentence before writing any code: 'dp[i] = the cheapest way to REACH step i, not yet having paid cost[i]'. Then ask 'where could the last move have come from?' — step i - 1 or step i - 2 — and the recurrence writes itself: dp[i] = min(dp[i-1] + cost[i-1], dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]). Base cases are the positions the question hands you for free: dp[0] = dp[1] = 0, because starting on either is allowed and costs nothing. Every DP in this section is that same three-part answer — state, recurrence, base cases — and pinning down the state first is what keeps the indices honest.

optimized.idea: Fill dp from the bottom. dp[i] is the cost to REACH step i, so dp[i] is not cost[i] — the price of step i is only paid when you leave it. The array needs n + 1 entries because the destination is the imaginary step just past the end, and dp[n] is the answer. Since each cell reads only the two before it, the whole table collapses into two variables.
code: int twoBack = 0;   // dp[i - 2]: cost to REACH that step, before paying to leave it
int oneBack = 0;   // dp[i - 1]; both are 0 because starting on step 0 or 1 is free
int current = Math.min(oneBack + cost[i - 1], twoBack + cost[i - 2]);
return oneBack;   // dp[n]: the floor past the last step

commonMistakes: Stopping the table at the last step — looping while i < n and returning dp[n - 1]. That is the cost to stand on the final step, not to get past it; on [10,15,20] it returns 10 instead of 15, and the answer is always short by exactly one hop.

Setting dp[1] = cost[0], reasoning that you must step on 0 before reaching 1. Starting on step 1 is explicitly allowed, so this forbids the cheaper start: [100,1,1,1] returns 101 instead of 2, and the error is invisible on inputs whose first element happens to be cheap.

Comparing cost[i - 1] against cost[i - 2] instead of the accumulated totals dp[i-1] + cost[i-1] and dp[i-2] + cost[i-2]. That is a greedy local choice wearing DP clothing: it passes [10,15,20] and then walks straight into the expensive stretch of [1,100,1,1,1,100,1,1,100,1], returning more than 6.
